claim_traces.claim_title: Humans only use 10% of their brains
claim_traces.claim_text: "Humans only use 10% of their brain capacity — the other 90% remains dormant and untapped."
reasoning_steps: The claim that humans only use 10% of their brain capacity is a widely debunked myth
Modern neuroscience has proven that humans use virtually all parts of their brains throughout the day

Neuroimaging technologies, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans, consistently show that even during sleep, nearly all areas of the brain exhibit some level of activity

Furthermore, evolutionary biology and medical science support this: brain tissue is metabolically expensive to maintain, and any unused or "dormant" brain regions would quickly atrophy (degenerate) or be weeded out by natural selection
Damage to almost any area of the brain results in significant functional deficits, confirming that there are no vast, untapped reservoirs of the brain.

claim_traces.claim_title: Great Wall of China visible from space
claim_traces.claim_text: "The Great Wall of China is the only man-made structure visible from space with the naked eye."
reasoning_steps: The claim that the Great Wall of China is the only man-made structure visible from space with the naked eye is a well-documented myth

According to NASA and reports from numerous astronauts (including China's own Yang Liwei), the Great Wall is virtually invisible to the naked eye from Low Earth Orbit (LEO) because it is narrow (generally less than 10 meters wide) and constructed of materials that closely match the color of the surrounding terrain
Conversely, other human-made structures, such as highways, airports, large dams, and cities (especially when illuminated at night), are visible from space.

claim_traces.claim_text: "Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short — around 5 feet 2 inches tall."
reasoning_steps: The claim that Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short and around 5 feet 2 inches tall is false
This popular myth stems from a misunderstanding of historical measurement systems
At his autopsy, Napoleon's height was recorded as 5 French feet and 2 French inches ("5 pieds 2 pouces")
Because a French foot (pied-du-roi) was longer than a British foot, this measurement actually converts to approximately 5 feet 6 inches (1.68 meters) in modern English units
In early 19th-century France, the average height for an adult male was about 5 feet 5 inches (1.65 meters)
Therefore, Napoleon was of average, or even slightly above-average, height for his era
The misconception was further fueled and popularized by British wartime propaganda, notably through the satirical caricatures of James Gillray, who depicted him as "Little Boney."

claim_traces.claim_title: Social media causes depression in teenagers
claim_traces.claim_text: "Social media use causes depression and anxiety in teenagers."
reasoning_steps: The claim that social media use causes depression and anxiety in teenagers is highly disputed among psychologists, epidemiologists, and social scientists

While there is a documented correlation between high social media use and poorer mental health outcomes in some adolescents, establishing a direct causal relationship remains a subject of intense scientific debate

On one side of the debate, researchers like Jonathan Haidt argue that the rapid rise of smartphones and social media in the early 2010s causally contributed to a global epidemic of teen mental illness, pointing to some experimental and longitudinal evidence

On the other side, researchers such as Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski argue that the vast majority of existing data is correlational, and meta-analyses suggest that the overall statistical effect size of social media on teen well-being is extremely small (accounting for less than 1% of the variance, comparable to minor daily variables like eating potatoes)

Furthermore, the direction of causality is unclear (e.g., depressed teens may turn to social media for coping), and impacts vary widely depending on whether usage is passive (scrolling) or active (socializing), as well as individual vulnerabilities
Because there is no scientific consensus on causation, the claim is classified as disputed.

claim_traces.claim_title: Generative AI will replace 300 million jobs
claim_traces.claim_text: "Generative AI will replace 300 million jobs worldwide."
reasoning_steps: The claim that generative AI "will replace 300 million jobs" is a misleading overstatement of the primary source from which it derives

The figure originates from a March 2023 Goldman Sachs report (by Jan Hatzius et al.), which estimated that generative AI could "expose" equivalent to roughly 300 million full-time jobs globally to automation
Crucially, the report distinguishes between being "exposed to" automation, being "complemented by" AI, and being "substituted" (replaced) by it
The economists noted that about two-thirds of current jobs are exposed to some degree of AI automation, but most of these would be complemented rather than fully replaced

Additionally, labor economics literature (including analyses by MIT and the Brookings Institution) highlights that technological shifts historically create new occupations and industries, meaning net job losses are not equivalent to the number of jobs exposed to automation.

claim_traces.claim_title: AI systems now pass the bar exam
claim_traces.claim_text: "AI language models can now pass the US bar examination at above-average scores."
reasoning_steps: The claim that AI language models can pass the US bar examination at above-average scores is true
In a widely cited 2023 study by researchers Daniel Martin Katz, Michael J
Bommarito II, and others, OpenAI's GPT-4 was evaluated on the Uniform Bar Examination (UBE)

GPT-4 achieved a score of 297, which comfortably exceeds the passing threshold of 270 required by even the most stringent US jurisdictions (such as New York and California, which requires a 1390/2000, equivalent to a similar high standard)

While the initial study placed GPT-4 in the 90th percentile (top 10%) of test-takers, a subsequent critique by Eric Martinez (MIT) suggested this comparison was overly optimistic because it compared GPT-4 against the less competitive February exam cohort

Martinez estimated that GPT-4's performance actually falls around the 68th percentile when compared to the more competitive July exam cohort, and around the 48th percentile among only those who passed

However, under both the original and revised analyses, GPT-4's score of 297 remains firmly above the average score of all test-takers (the 50th percentile), and its ability to pass the exam is undisputed
Subsequent models, such as Claude 3 and newer iterations of GPT, have continued to demonstrate comparable or superior capabilities on legal examinations.

claim_traces.claim_title: US Congress passed no budget on time since 1997
claim_traces.claim_text: "The US Congress has not passed a complete federal budget on time since 1997."
reasoning_steps: According to historical records from the Congressional Research Service (CRS) and the Pew Research Center, the U.S
Congress has not passed all of its individual, regular appropriations bills on time (before the October 1 start of the fiscal year) since Fiscal Year 1997
For FY 1997, the final appropriations bills were enacted on September 30, 1996

Since then (FY 1998 to the present), Congress has consistently failed to meet the October 1 deadline for all of its federal spending bills, instead relying on Continuing Resolutions (CRs) to temporarily fund the government and subsequently passing omnibus packages or consolidated appropriations long after the fiscal year has started.
